about: Simulator: energy flow up a food chain (GPP, producer respiration and NPP, the fraction stored at each level, respiration heat, energy to decomposers), energy and biomass pyramids, and a biomagnification mode for a persistent toxin. Model code: bio/assets/tools/bio-tool-math.js (ApBioMath.energyFlow). Validator: scripts/lib/apbio-tool-checks/energy-flow.mjs checks each rule through the model (NPP = GPP − respiration, the stored fraction, energy conservation, an inverted biomass pyramid for the open-water chain, the toxin's rise per level) and recomputes every number in the stimulus tables and the numeric answer.
intro: Follow the energy that producers capture up a food chain. Set how much energy the producers capture, how much each level passes on and how much is burned in cellular respiration, then add or remove a level and compare the pyramids of energy and of biomass. A second mode follows a toxin that the body cannot break down. In a food web, each level groups every species that feeds at that step. The questions below use the same model.
howItWorks:
Every number is energy per square meter of ground or water surface per year (kcal/m²/yr) unless it says otherwise.

  1. Producers capture light energy in photosynthesis. All the energy they capture is the gross primary productivity (GPP).
  2. Producers use part of it in their own cellular respiration, which releases it as heat. What is left, stored in new producer tissue, is the net primary productivity (NPP): NPP = GPP − producer respiration. NPP is the base of the energy pyramid and all the energy the consumers can get.
  3. Each consumer level stores only a fraction of the energy the level below stored (the fraction passed on; about 10% is typical, the "10% rule"). Part of the level below is never eaten, or is eaten but not absorbed (it leaves in feces); that energy goes to decomposers. Of what a consumer level does absorb, most is used in cellular respiration to move, keep warm and repair cells, and it leaves as heat.
  4. So the energy stored shrinks at every step up, and a pyramid of energy always narrows upward. Energy flows one way: heat cannot be captured again by producers.

The model's rules:

  • Producers: respiration = (producer respiration share) × GPP; NPP = GPP − respiration.
  • Each consumer level: energy stored = (fraction passed on) × energy stored by the level below. To store that, the level must absorb energy stored ÷ (1 − respiration share), because the respiration share of everything it absorbs leaves as heat. The rest of the level below's stored energy goes to decomposers. The respiration share cannot be more than 1 − the fraction passed on, since a level cannot absorb more than the level below stored.
  • Top level: all its stored energy eventually goes to decomposers. Decomposers' own respiration also ends as heat; the model counts their share separately. Every kcal of GPP ends as heat or with decomposers.
  • Biomass (grams of dry mass per m², at one moment) = energy stored per year ÷ 4 kcal per gram ÷ how many times a year that level's biomass is replaced. Plankton are replaced many times a year, so in open water a small mass of producers can feed a larger mass of consumers: the biomass pyramid can be upside down, even though the energy pyramid never is.
  • A persistent toxin (for example, the pesticide DDT, or mercury in the form fish store) is not broken down and is barely excreted, so a consumer keeps the toxin from all the food it absorbs (the retained share; 100% keeps all of it). Because most of that food is burned in respiration while the toxin stays, the toxin is concentrated: concentration = food's concentration × retained share ÷ (1 − respiration share), at every level.
  • All values are illustrative, chosen to show the patterns. There is no chance: the same settings always give the same numbers.

ef-s1.title: Energy and biomass in two food chains
ef-s1.text: A student used the model for two food chains with the same settings: producers capture the same energy, use half of it in their own respiration, each consumer level stores 10% of the energy stored by the level below, and consumers use 80% of the energy they absorb in cellular respiration. Table 1 is a grassland and Table 2 is the open ocean, where phytoplankton (microscopic algae) are replaced about 200 times a year. In Table 3, a pesticide that is not broken down enters the grassland food chain; consumers keep all of the pesticide in the food they absorb. Energy values are in kcal/m²/yr.

tables.caption: Table 1. Grassland food chain
cols: Energy lost as heat in respiration (kcal/m²/yr)

tables.caption: Table 3. Pesticide in the grassland food chain

questions.q: Using Table 1, calculate the gross primary productivity (GPP) of the grassland's producers, in kcal/m²/yr.

why.correct: The energy stored in new producer tissue is the net primary productivity, and NPP = GPP − producer respiration. So GPP = NPP + respiration = 10,000 + 10,000 = 20,000 kcal/m²/yr.

questions.q: In Table 1, the grasshoppers store 1,000 kcal/m²/yr, but the frogs that eat them store only 100 kcal/m²/yr. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?
options: Most of the energy the frogs absorb is used in cellular respiration and leaves as heat, and part of the grasshoppers is never eaten or absorbed and goes to decomposers
The frogs return most of the energy they absorb to the grasses, which use it again in photosynthesis
Energy is destroyed when the frogs digest grasshoppers, so only a tenth of it still exists afterward
The frogs turn most of the energy they absorb into body mass, but the mass is lost when they die

why.correct: Energy is not destroyed; it changes form. Of the grasshoppers' 1,000 kcal, the frogs absorb only part (the rest goes to decomposers), and of what they absorb, 80% powers cellular respiration and leaves the food chain as heat (400 kcal/m²/yr in Table 1). Only the remainder, 100 kcal/m²/yr, is stored in new frog tissue that the next level could eat.
options: Right: respiration heat and the share never eaten or absorbed account for the 900 kcal that is not stored.
Heat released by respiration cannot be captured by producers; energy flows one way through a food chain, while matter is recycled.
Energy is conserved: the missing 900 kcal still exists, mostly as heat and as energy taken up by decomposers.
Table 1 shows the frogs losing more energy as heat (400 kcal) than they store as tissue (100 kcal), so most absorbed energy does not become body mass.

questions.q: In Table 2, the phytoplankton have a smaller biomass than the zooplankton that eat them, yet they store ten times more energy each year. Which explanation is most consistent with the data?
options: Phytoplankton reproduce and are eaten so quickly that a small standing mass makes a large amount of new tissue over a year
Zooplankton capture light energy too, so they need less energy from phytoplankton
Energy passes from zooplankton back down to phytoplankton, so the energy pyramid is inverted along with the biomass pyramid
Each gram of phytoplankton holds far less energy than a gram of zooplankton, so the same energy weighs less

why.correct: Biomass is the mass present at one moment; stored energy is a rate over a year. Phytoplankton are replaced about 200 times a year, so the 12.5 g/m² present at any moment adds up to 10,000 kcal/m²/yr of new tissue. Zooplankton are replaced only about 10 times a year, so more of their mass is present at once. The energy pyramid stays upright: 10,000 then 1,000 kcal/m²/yr.
options: Right: a fast turnover lets a small biomass of producers support a larger biomass of consumers.
Zooplankton are consumers; they get their energy by eating phytoplankton, not from light.
Table 2 shows the energy stored falling at every level (10,000 then 1,000 then 100), so the energy pyramid is upright and energy flows only upward.
The model uses the same energy per gram (4 kcal) at every level; the difference comes from how fast each level is replaced.

questions.q: In Table 3, the pesticide concentration is five times higher at each trophic level than in the level below. Which explanation is most consistent with the model?
options: A consumer burns most of the food it absorbs in respiration but keeps the pesticide, so the pesticide from a large mass of food ends up in a small mass of tissue
The pesticide is made inside each consumer's cells, so organisms higher in the chain make more of it
Consumers absorb the pesticide directly from the soil, and larger animals take up more of it
The pesticide is passed on at 10% per level, the same as energy, so it builds up at the top

why.correct: The pesticide is not broken down or excreted. With 80% of absorbed food used in respiration, a consumer builds 1 g of tissue from 5 g of absorbed food and keeps the pesticide from all 5 g, so its concentration is 5 times its food's: 0.04, 0.20, 1.00, then 5.00 parts per million. This build-up up a food chain is biomagnification.
options: Right: the food's mass leaves as carbon dioxide and water in respiration while the pesticide stays behind.
The pesticide comes from outside and enters through the producers; consumers take it in with their food.
In the model the only route in for consumers is their food, and the concentration rises by the same factor at every level whatever the animal's size.
If the pesticide were passed on like energy, its amount would shrink up the chain; it is concentrated because it is kept while the food is burned.

questions.q: The student adds hawks that eat the snakes as a fifth level to the grassland in Table 1, with the same settings. Which prediction is most consistent with the model?
options: The hawks would store about 1 kcal/m²/yr, so the land could support very few hawks, which helps explain why food chains rarely have more than four or five levels
The hawks would store about 100 kcal/m²/yr, because a new level starts again from the energy the producers capture
The hawks would store about 10 kcal/m²/yr, the same as the snakes, because energy stays constant at the top of a chain
Adding the hawks would raise the energy stored by the producers, because more consumers recycle more energy

why.correct: Each level stores 10% of the level below: 10% of the snakes' 10 kcal/m²/yr is 1 kcal/m²/yr. So little energy reaches a fifth level that only a sparse population of large predators can be supported, which limits the length of food chains.
options: Right: 10% of 10 kcal/m²/yr is 1 kcal/m²/yr, too little to support many predators.
A level gets energy only from the level it eats, so the hawks' share comes from the snakes, not from the producers directly.
The fraction passed on applies at every step, including the last, so the hawks would store a tenth of what the snakes store.
The producers' energy comes from light (GPP); adding a consumer level does not change it, and energy is not recycled.

frq.title: Mini free-response question: where the energy goes

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: In a different meadow, producers capture 8,000 kcal/m²/yr (GPP) and use 3,500 kcal/m²/yr in their own respiration. Calculate the meadow's net primary productivity. Then calculate the energy stored by its secondary consumers, if each level stores 10% of the energy stored by the level below.

rubric.point: Calculates the secondary consumers' stored energy as 4,500 × 0.1 × 0.1 = 45 kcal/m²/yr (450 for the primary consumers first). Accept a correct value carried from an incorrect NPP.

parts.sample: NPP = GPP − producer respiration = 8,000 − 3,500 = 4,500 kcal/m²/yr. Primary consumers store 10% of that, 450 kcal/m²/yr, and secondary consumers store 10% of 450, which is 45 kcal/m²/yr.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: In Table 1, the snakes' biomass (5 g/m²) is far smaller than the grasses' (2,500 g/m²). Explain why there is so much less biomass at the top of the food chain.

rubric.point: Explains that at each step most energy is lost as heat in cellular respiration (or goes uneaten to decomposers), so much less energy reaches each higher level to build tissue, and less energy supports less biomass.
accept: only about 10% of energy is stored at each level, the rest is lost as heat
less energy available means fewer or smaller organisms can be supported

parts.sample: At every step up the chain, most of the energy a level absorbs is used in cellular respiration and lost as heat, and part of each level is never eaten. Only about 10% of the energy is stored in the next level's tissue, so the snakes receive a tiny fraction of the grasses' energy, too little to build or support a large mass of snakes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Frogs are ectotherms: they warm their bodies mainly with heat from the environment. Suppose the frogs in Table 1 were replaced by shrews, endotherms that keep their bodies warm with heat from their own respiration, absorbing the same energy from the grasshoppers. Predict how the energy available to the snakes would change. Justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts less energy for the snakes, and justifies it: endotherms use a larger share of the energy they absorb in respiration to make body heat, so less of it is stored in new tissue that the snakes can eat.
accept: decrease, because shrews burn more energy keeping warm
less, since more of the absorbed energy is lost as heat

parts.sample: The snakes would get less energy. Shrews hold their body temperature with heat from their own cellular respiration, so they use a larger share of the energy they absorb in respiration than frogs do. With the same energy absorbed, less is left to store in new shrew tissue, and that stored energy is all the snakes can get from eating them.
